definition: The Computer Science Ontology (CSO) is an automatically generated taxonomy of research topics in the field of Computer Science.
details: It was produced by the Open University in collaboration with Springer Nature by running an information extraction system over a large corpus of scientific articles. Several branches were manually improved by domain experts. The current version (CSO 3.2) includes about 14K research topics and 160K semantic relationships. CSO is available in OWL, Turtle, and N-Triples. It is aligned with several other knowledge graphs, including DBpedia, Wikidata, YAGO, Freebase, and Cyc. New versions of CSO are regularly released on the CSO Portal. CSO is mostly used to characterise scientific papers and other documents according to their research areas, in order to enable different kinds of analytics. The CSO Classifier is an open-source python tool for automatically annotating documents with CSO.

explainer.lead: The Computer Science Ontology (CSO) is a large, structured map of computer science research topics and the relationships between them. It gives papers and other documents a shared set of research-area labels, making them easier to classify, compare, and analyse.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a huge family tree for computer science ideas, showing which topics belong together and how they connect. CSO is that kind of map, built by reading many scientific articles with software and improved in places by experts. It helps computers label research documents so people can find patterns across them.
tiers.practitioner: Use CSO as a controlled topic vocabulary when annotating papers or other documents by research area. The open-source Python CSO Classifier automates this annotation, while CSO itself is available in OWL, Turtle, and N-Triples for knowledge-graph workflows. Keep the ontology and classifier distinct, and check the version because new releases appear regularly on the CSO Portal.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, CSO can be viewed as CSO = (T, R), where T is a taxonomy of computer science research topics and R is a set of semantic relationships between them. Version 3.2 contains about 14K topics and 160K relationships, produced through information extraction over scientific articles with manual refinement of several branches. Its alignments include DBpedia, Wikidata, YAGO, Freebase, and Cyc; automatic generation means its construction is not wholly expert-curated.

explainer.example: A research paper about neural networks is passed to the CSO Classifier, which annotates it with relevant CSO research topics. Those annotations allow it to be grouped with other papers in the same research areas and included in topic-based analytics.

explainer.intuition: CSO provides a common map of research topics so that different documents can be described in the same terms. Its semantic relationships add structure beyond a flat list of keywords.
howItWorks: An information extraction system processes a large corpus of scientific articles.
The extracted topics and relationships form the CSO taxonomy.
Domain experts manually improve several branches.
Documents are annotated with CSO topics, either directly or with the CSO Classifier.
The resulting labels support research-area analytics.
explainer.whyItMatters: A shared, structured vocabulary makes research-area annotations more consistent across large document collections. CSO also connects this vocabulary to other knowledge graphs and provides an open-source classifier for applying it automatically.
misconceptions: CSO is not entirely hand-built: it is automatically generated, with selected branches improved by experts.
CSO is the ontology; the CSO Classifier is the separate tool that applies it to documents.
It is a taxonomy of research topics, not a collection of full research papers.
